name: Demi Guard
description: Demi Guard is Keenan Cornelius' gi lapel guard against forward pressure. Learn its collar grip, foot-on-lapel control, sweep options and passing priorities.
variant_uniqueness: Foot on lapel supports a knee-line barrier
summary: Demi Guard is a gi lapel guard that combines a collar grip, the opponent's lapel behind their knee, and a foot pressing on the lapel tail to resist pressure and create elevation.
overview:
Keenan Cornelius introduces Demi Guard as an answer to a passer driving forward after a worm-wrestling attempt. The bottom player's foot has left the worm configuration, so rebuilding that guard may be difficult. Demi supplies a different connection at the knee rather than requiring the original wrap to be restored. See [Keenan's introduction](https://jiujitsux.com/courses/keenans-lapel-encyclopedia/lesson/16-1-introduction-to-the-demi-guard/).

[Legion's dictionary](https://legionsandiego.com/the-jiu-jitsu-dictionary/#demi-guard) describes the collar grip, lapel behind the passer's knee, and foot on the lapel tail. The guard player stays in front of the passer with bent legs between their bodies; the fabric supports the foot's work against pressure. The top player must deal with that connection while keeping balance.

Demi belongs with [[Positions/Lapel Guard]] and connects to [[Positions/Worm Guard]]. It is distinct from [[Positions/Half Guard]], whose defining control is trapping one opponent's leg between both legs. Half guard can be a recovery destination after releasing the lapel structure. A lapel is essential to Demi, so this position has no no-gi equivalent. Back takes and submissions are follow-ups through recovered guards, not automatic results of holding Demi.

disambiguations.name: Half Guard
disambiguations.reason: Demi uses a collar grip and foot-on-lapel knee control; Half Guard traps one leg between both legs and also exists in no-gi.

key_principles: Recognize the collar, knee-line lapel and foot as a connected guard structure.
Keep the legs between the players while the top player presses forward.
Use the lapel connection to create room and elevation, not to twist a trapped knee.
Distinguish a completed guard configuration from merely holding loose fabric.
Recover another guard when the foot-on-lapel connection is lost.
Clear the lapel and leg barrier before treating a passing attempt as complete.

top.name: Demi Guard Top
top.description: Recognize Demi Guard from top, protect your balance, clear the foot-on-lapel connection and distinguish a guard reset from a completed pass.
top.overview:
You are the passer above an opponent who has connected your collar and knee line with your own lapel. Their foot presses on the lapel tail, and their bent legs remain between your bodies. Driving forward can load that structure instead of bringing you closer to a pass. Keep a usable base while addressing the fabric and foot connection.

Clearing the lapel may leave you facing [[Positions/Open Guard]] or caught in [[Positions/Half Guard]]. Neither is a completed pass. Advance to [[Positions/Side Control]] only after clearing the legs and controlling the upper body. The defensive priorities here are applications of the published configuration; they do not claim to reproduce an unavailable Demi passing lesson.
state_invariants: The top player's torso faces the bottom player while one knee is controlled by the lapel running behind it.
The bottom player's bent legs remain in front of the passer, with one foot pressing against the lapel tail.
The collar grip connects the passer's upper body to the guard player while the passer still has space to adjust base.
prerequisites: Your opponent has established the collar and knee-line lapel connections.
Their foot remains engaged with the lapel tail.
You are still facing a guard rather than holding a completed pin.
key_principles: Keep balance while identifying the loaded foot and fabric.
Reduce the lapel connection before committing forward weight.
Move the controlled leg only when the fabric permits it.
Recognize a remaining leg trap as half guard.
Complete leg clearance before settling a side-control pin.

decision_tree.condition: The foot-on-lapel barrier is intact and prevents a safe passing step
You can clear the fabric and control the legs without losing balance
The bottom player starts elevating your controlled knee

common_errors.error: Driving into the intact lapel barrier
common_errors.consequence: Your weight loads the guard player's elevation structure.
common_errors.correction: Restore balance and address the foot and fabric first.

common_errors.error: Pulling the controlled knee free by force
common_errors.consequence: The remaining wrap can bind the leg during the movement.
common_errors.correction: Loosen the fabric before moving the controlled leg.

common_errors.consequence: The foot-on-lapel connection remains active below you.
common_errors.correction: Track the collar, foot and knee-line connection together.

common_errors.error: Treating a cleared lapel as a finished pass
common_errors.consequence: The opponent's legs can still retain an ordinary guard.
common_errors.correction: Check whether a leg trap or open-guard frame remains.

common_errors.error: Reaching with both hands while losing base
common_errors.consequence: The bottom player can redirect your unsupported weight.
common_errors.correction: Keep a stable base throughout the grip-clearing exchange.

training_drills.name: Connection recognition
training_drills.description: Begin in a cooperative Demi configuration. Name the collar grip, lapel path and loaded foot, then reset before attempting to clear any of them.

training_drills.name: Clear and stop
training_drills.description: Start with light lapel tension. Clear the connection while the partner retains ordinary leg frames; stop at open guard and check that neither knee is bound.

training_drills.name: Pass or reset
training_drills.description: Begin in Demi with light resistance. Attempt the clear and pass; reset on side control, a sweep, or a recovered guard. Stop immediately on discomfort.

flashcards.question: What should you address before driving through Demi Guard?
flashcards.answer: Address the foot-on-lapel connection while maintaining your balance; forward pressure can otherwise load the opponent's elevation.

flashcards.question: What tells you that a lapel clear has not yet passed Demi Guard?
flashcards.answer: The bottom player's legs still frame between you or trap one leg, leaving open guard or half guard instead of side control.

flashcards.question: Why should you avoid twisting a knee caught in the Demi lapel connection?
flashcards.answer: The fabric can keep the leg bound while your body turns; release the tension before moving the controlled knee.

flashcards.question: Which upper-body grip should you monitor against Demi Guard?
flashcards.answer: Monitor the bottom player's collar grip together with the knee-line lapel and foot, rather than watching only one connection.

flashcards.question: What is your priority when Demi Guard begins to elevate you?
flashcards.answer: Recover a stable base and reduce the loaded connection before trying to continue the passing movement.

flashcards.question: When has a pass from Demi Guard reached side control?
flashcards.answer: Both leg barriers have been cleared and you control the opponent's upper body from the side, without a remaining half-guard trap.

bottom.name: Demi Guard Bottom
bottom.description: Maintain Demi Guard's collar and foot-on-lapel connections, recognize forward pressure for elevation, and recover half guard or another lapel guard when needed.
bottom.overview:
You face the passer from underneath with the lapel routed behind their knee, a collar grip controlling their upper body, and a foot pressing on the lapel tail. Keep your knees in front of your torso so the connection can support distance and elevation. Having the lapel in your hand alone does not establish Demi Guard.

Use the passer's pressure as the cue for [[Transitions/Demi Guard Elevation Sweep]]. If the fabric or foot connection stops working, recover [[Positions/Half Guard]] or return to [[Positions/Lapel Guard]] before chasing another attack. The latter has existing back-take, omoplata and triangle setups; those require a new position and their own controls. Do not treat the word Demi as another name for ordinary half guard.
state_invariants: The bottom player faces the passer with bent knees between their torsos rather than allowing chest-to-chest side control.
The passer's lapel runs behind the controlled knee and reaches the bottom player's foot, which presses on its tail.
The bottom player maintains a collar grip and a working lapel connection so the foot can help manage pressure at the knee line.
prerequisites: The opponent wears a gi with an accessible lapel.
You can keep your legs between the players while arranging the grips.
There is space to route the lapel behind the knee and place the foot on its tail.
key_principles: Keep the collar and knee-line connections working together.
Place the foot on the lapel tail rather than merely holding loose cloth.
Keep bent legs between you and the passer.
Read forward pressure before attempting elevation.
Recover another guard promptly when the Demi connection is lost.

decision_tree.condition: The passer's weight comes forward over your working lapel connection
The passer retreats and you retain useful lapel control
The foot-on-lapel control fails but one opponent's leg remains within reach

common_errors.error: Holding fabric without engaging the foot
common_errors.consequence: The characteristic knee-line barrier is incomplete.
common_errors.correction: Confirm the lapel path and foot contact before relying on Demi.

common_errors.error: Letting both knees drift behind the passer
common_errors.consequence: The passer can approach your torso without a leg barrier.
common_errors.correction: Recover your legs in front before attempting another lapel feed.

common_errors.error: Trying to lift a balanced opponent with the arms
common_errors.consequence: The grips tire without creating a useful change of base.
common_errors.correction: Wait for or create a visible weight shift before elevation.

common_errors.error: Hanging onto a lost lapel while being passed
common_errors.consequence: The grip occupies a hand needed for frames and recovery.
common_errors.correction: Release the ineffective connection and recover a guard.

common_errors.error: Keeping the lapel bound after coming on top
common_errors.consequence: The same connection can obstruct your own stabilization.
common_errors.correction: Release unnecessary fabric and establish the actual landing position.

training_drills.name: Build and identify
training_drills.description: From seated open guard, arrange the collar, knee-line lapel and foot contact with a cooperative partner. Identify all three before releasing and resetting.

training_drills.name: Pressure recognition
training_drills.description: With light grips, let the passer alternate forward pressure and retreat. Name the sweep or recovery opportunity; reset without forcing a loaded knee.

training_drills.name: Guard recovery exchange
training_drills.description: Start in Demi and allow a gradual lapel clear. Recover half guard or another lapel configuration; stop and reset when the destination is stable or the passer clears both legs.

related_content.name: Demi Guard to Half Guard

submission_probability.description: The listed Demi transitions contain no direct finish. Submission routes continue through other established positions.

flashcards.question: Where does your foot contact the fabric in Demi Guard?
flashcards.answer: The foot presses on the tail of the opponent's lapel after that lapel has been routed behind their knee.

flashcards.question: What upper-body grip accompanies the foot-on-lapel control?
flashcards.answer: A collar grip connects the opponent's upper body to your guard while the lapel and foot control their knee line.

flashcards.question: Which passer reaction creates Demi Guard's elevation opportunity?
flashcards.answer: Forward pressure can bring the passer's weight onto the working lapel connection, providing an opportunity to elevate and reverse.

flashcards.question: What should you recover if the foot-on-lapel connection is lost?
flashcards.answer: Recover a guard that still fits the available controls, such as half guard around one leg or a usable lapel guard in front.

flashcards.question: Why keep your knees between you and the passer in Demi Guard?
flashcards.answer: The legs supply the barrier that lets the lapel connection help manage distance; a loose grip alone does not prevent a pass.

flashcards.question: What must change after a Demi elevation brings you on top?
flashcards.answer: Free any fabric that obstructs movement and stabilize the landing, recognizing whether the opponent still holds half or open guard.

flashcards_position.question: Which uniform is required for Demi Guard?
flashcards_position.answer: Demi Guard requires a gi because the opponent's lapel supplies the fabric connection behind the knee and under the foot.

flashcards_position.question: What are the three defining connections in Demi Guard?
flashcards_position.answer: A collar grip, the opponent's lapel behind their knee, and a foot pressing on the lapel tail form the defining configuration.

flashcards_position.question: Which pressure problem does Keenan's Demi Guard address?
flashcards_position.answer: It addresses a passer driving forward, including the reaction that stops a worm-wrestling attempt after the original leg wrap has been left.

flashcards_position.question: How is Demi Guard different from ordinary Half Guard?
flashcards_position.answer: Demi is defined by a collar and foot-on-lapel structure, while ordinary half guard traps one opponent's leg between both legs.

flashcards_position.question: Which player is on top in Demi Guard?
flashcards_position.answer: The passer is the top player; the bottom player maintains the collar, lapel and leg structure while seeking a sweep or guard recovery.

flashcards_position.question: What separates a Demi Guard sweep from a submission finish?
flashcards_position.answer: A sweep changes which player is on top and still requires stabilization; it does not by itself end the exchange with a tap.
